newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian police end Venice belltower protest
newsitem.headline: Italian police end Venice belltower protest

text.p: Police commandos stormed the belltower in St Mark's Square in Venice on Friday and arrested eight Italian separatists who had occupied the landmark in a bizarre bid for an independent state in the lagoon city.

Masked paramilitary Carabinieri special forces ended the protest without firing a shot some five hours after the group of young men, many of them dressed in combat fatigues, broke into the monument, one of the best-known symbols of Venice.

Police said the group had commandeered a "vaporetto" ferry shortly after midnight to take them, a six-wheeled home-made armoured vehicle and a camper van down the Grand Canal to St Mark's Square, a magnet for millions of tourists.
The police scaled part of the outside of the 99 metre (325 foot) tower by telescopic ladder. They entered through a low level balcony and used an internal staircase to the top.
"Our main objective was to avoid using weapons. They gave themselves up without any resistance," a senior Carabinieri police officer said.
Some of the protesters, who police confirmed numbered eight, were arrested in the tower and others were seized in the square below in their black and green armoured vehicle and the van, police said.
One shouted "Long Live St Mark" in a Venetian accent as police led him off to cries from onlookers of "Shame" and "You should be thrown in the lagoon".
Police earlier said they believed the protesters were armed but it was not clear whether any weapons had been found.
Police and the main separatist party in Italy, the Northern League, separately described the protest as madness.
"Finding an armoured car and going to St Mark's Square to stand there and raise a little flag is no way to stage a revolution," League leader Umberto Bossi told Italian radio.
Other politicians, however, argued that the protest pointed to a deeper malaise in northern Italy at the lack of movement towards federal reform.
"These are confusing times in the north, confusing enough to spark provocations in minds that are not very mature," Venice mayor Massimo Cacciari, a leftist, told Reuters.
"This has nothing to do with the League but with a general climate of confusion which leads some crazy people to do something as insane and dangerous as this," he said.

The group had hoisted a banner bearing the symbol of the Lion of St Mark from the top of the tower and issued a statement describing themselves as a regular unit of the army of the "Most Serene Republic of Venice".

"After 200 years, a regular unit of the Most Serene Venetian Army has tonight liberated St Mark's Square," the statement said. "The Most Serene Republic of Venice has been reborn today...Long live St Mark."
Police linked Friday's protest to a shadowy group that has interrupted state television news bulletins in the northeast Veneto region for two months with calls for a separate state.
The pirate broadcasts have spoken of a "spectacular action" in the canal city to mark next Monday's 200th anniversary of the fall of the Venice Republic.

Venice was for centuries a powerful independent power with territories stretching down the Adriatic and into the Middle East. Known as the "Most Serene Republic" it came to an end on May 12, 1797, when French forces of Napoleon Bonaparte entered the city.
Separatist sentiment has grown in affluent northern Italy in the 1990s, spurred first by political corruption scandals and later by resentment at high taxes and central bureaucracy.

The Northern League last September declared a symbolic republic of "Padania" at a rally in Venice but Bossi's drive has cost him popular support, driven home by the loss of control of Italy's financial capital, Milan, in local elections on April 27.
